name: Routines, Schedules, and Social Stories
title: Routines, Schedules, and Social Stories
answer: This idea is that young children, especially those with autism or anxiety, benefit from knowing what comes next through picture schedules, visual routines, and short social stories. Teachers can use tools such as Boardmaker and Canva for Education, and general tools can draft the words, so a story about a fire drill, a new classmate, or a dentist visit can be ready the same day. It matters because these supports reduce uncertainty for children and can also travel home as translated picture routines that families find useful.

sections.body: Young children do better when they know what comes next. Picture schedules, visual routines, and short social stories that explain a new experience help many children, especially those with autism or anxiety. The problem this solves is the uncertainty and worry that can come with a new event or a change in routine. Tools such as Boardmaker and Canva for Education let teachers build these supports quickly, and general tools can draft the words. A social story about a fire drill, a new classmate, or a visit to the dentist can be ready the same day it is needed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the preschool through second grade band, the teacher tailors each social story or visual routine to the child or class. A social story should use simple, positive language, describe what will happen and how the child might feel, and suggest what the child can do. AI drafts often need to be shortened and softened for this age. The special education teacher or counselor should review stories written for a specific child. Visual supports also help families, so a picture routine for getting ready in the morning or going to bed can go home with a child and be translated into the family's language.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. It does report that families often say these small supports make the biggest difference at home. It also states that these supports cost almost nothing to make and can be updated whenever a routine changes. Those are practical claims from the book, not research findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how these tools should be used. AI drafts often need to be shortened and softened for young children, so a person must edit them before use. The teacher tailors each story or routine to the child or class, and the special education teacher or counselor should review stories written for a specific child. The decisions about what a child needs, what language is simple and positive, and what a story should suggest the child can do stay with the people who know the child. Families also need the routine translated into their language when it goes home.
